name: AppLess (Thesys)
what: Experimental demo of a phone with no apps - every screen generated by an LLM on demand, streamed, and rendered as real native components (Cupertino/Material 3) via the OpenUI spec. Expo SDK 54 / React Native, Cerebras for generation.
priceDetail: Free / MIT. Needs a Cerebras API key. The commercial upstream (Thesys OpenUI Cloud / C1 API) is priced separately.
notes: Generative UI - an LLM emitting a constrained component contract that renders in your own design system rather than free-form HTML - is the pattern most likely to matter for your design-system and Foundry work.
Reproducing the demo is the wrong thing to build. The reusable asset is the schema-constrained render contract, worth prototyping against Foundry's design tokens. The phone-OS framing is a tech demo.

Read as a pattern study, not a dependency. 4 commits and no releases means no maintenance story, and the integrations are simulated. Needs a Cerebras API key. The serious upstream is thesysdev/openui plus Thesys's commercial OpenUI Cloud / C1 API - price that separately before building a client feature on it.
adminNote: Read as a pattern study. The reusable asset is the schema-constrained render contract, not the phone-OS demo.

name: GatherOS
what: Local-first macOS app for capturing, organising and searching design references - drag, paste and screenshot capture, X bookmark sync, AI visual search, colour search, auto-tagging, unlimited libraries, and Figma-like open-canvas 'Spaces' for moodboarding. Companion Chrome extension saves from X, Instagram, Cosmos and any page.
priceDetail: Free while in public beta. Paid pricing not announced - assume a paid tier lands when beta ends.
notes: Solid for the studio's reference and moodboard workflow feeding concept and design-system work, but single-machine and Mac-only so it will not serve as a shared team library.
A native Mac app with local storage, browser extension, social sync and AI visual and colour search is months of work in a stack you probably do not want to own.

'Free' is a beta state, not a commitment - paid pricing has not been announced, so do not build a team process on it yet. Real limitations: macOS only, no web or mobile, no cloud sync (library lives on one machine, so no team sharing and backup is your problem), no semantic search, no agent or MCP integration. Small user base but actively maintained and pre-1.0.

name: meat (Bold Software)
what: Go CLI that uses a model to abridge a code diff into a 'reading diff' - stripping style and nil-check noise so a reviewer sees only conceptual and architectural changes. Explicitly aimed at humans reviewing agent-generated code.
priceDetail: Free / Apache 2.0. Real cost is model tokens on large diffs - verify before putting in CI.
notes: If you ship AI-written code for clients, this attacks the main quality bottleneck in that workflow - reviewing large agent diffs.
The mechanism is a chunked diff-splitter plus a well-tuned prompt - reproducible in a day. The only real asset is prompt quality, so use theirs rather than reinvent it.

14 stars means a credible experiment from a strong team (same org as sketch.dev), not a maintained product. README warns processing a commit takes a while and multi-MB diffs are chunked, so cost and latency scale with diff size. Which model/API key it needs is not documented - verify token spend before putting it in CI.
adminNote: Try the Apache-2.0 tool before writing our own. Verify model cost on large diffs.

name: oil-motion
what: NOT a JavaScript motion library despite the name. It is an agent Skill for Claude Code that designs an interactive animation, generates keyframe images, calls an AI video model for the in-between motion, compresses the result into web assets (WebP sprite sheets, MP4, frame sequences) and maps playback 0-100% to scroll, pointer, drag, touch, orientation or audio.
priceDetail: Free / MIT to use. Real cost is per-render AI video credits via ZenMux (MiniMax) - budget this per project.
notes: A genuinely new capability - art-directed, semantic motion for scroll-driven hero sections that you currently cannot produce without a motion designer.
MIT and installable as a skill in an afternoon. Rebuilding means a video-gen pipeline plus ffmpeg frame processing plus a scroll-mapped runtime, for no commercial upside.

Do not let this get mis-sold internally as a Motion/GSAP replacement. Those animate live DOM properties with tiny payloads; oil-motion animates pre-rendered pixels, so the deliverable is video or sprite sheets - heavy, not responsive, not screen-reader accessible, not text-selectable, cannot adapt to dynamic content or theming. No bundle-size claim anywhere, which is telling. Single maintainer, days-old code, primary SKILL.md is in Chinese, hard dependency on a paid third-party API, and needs Python 3, Pillow, ffmpeg and ffprobe locally. Specialist asset generator for one-off hero moments only - budget the render spend into the quote. Star count came from Trendshift and SkillsMP, not the repo header, which rendered inconsistently.

name: Originkit
what: Free animated component library ('largest free animated component library'), React and Framer variants, copy directly or pull via MCP. The link filters to the text-animation category.
priceDetail: Free. No paid tier, but also no licence published - treat that as a blocker for client work.
notes: Useful as a free grab-bag of text and animation effects for marketing-site builds, but too shallow and unproven to base a repeatable component pipeline on.
Individual text-animation effects are a few hours each with Motion or CSS. Take inspiration and the odd effect, not a dependency.

Thinnest item in the batch. No licence, attribution terms, component count or team disclosed anywhere on the site - no licence means no clear right to ship these in client work, so treat that as a blocker until confirmed. Framer-first positioning suggests the React exports are secondary. Effects skew showy rather than production-useful. Transitions.dev is the serious option.

name: ui.camera
what: Free browser tool that turns flat UI screenshots into 'product photography for software' - upload an image, manipulate 3D rotation on X/Y/Z, aspect ratio, aperture and depth of field, autofocus and zoom, then capture and export PNG.
priceDetail: Free. No pricing, tiers or sign-in anywhere on the site; monetisation model undisclosed.
notes: Useful for dressing up client app screenshots in case studies, proposals and your own portfolio without a designer mocking things up in Figma or Blender.

A WebGL plane with a texture, perspective camera controls, a shader depth-of-field pass and canvas export. A competent front-end dev could ship a rough version in a weekend - but it is free, so there is no reason to.

No about page, footer, credits, company name or social handle anywhere - the maker is genuinely unidentified, so provenance and longevity are unknown. Maximum-quality export requires their Chrome extension downloaded as a raw ZIP rather than from the Chrome Web Store, which means manual unpacked install, no store review and no auto-updates. Given it will need page-capture permissions, think twice before installing it on a machine holding client work. The in-browser version needs no install and is the safer default.

name: Flaude
what: Figma-side tool that copies real app screens and multi-step flows into Figma as editable layers rather than flat screenshots, then lets you redesign them via a Claude MCP connection. The /browse page is the free library of hundreds of web and iOS screens from Uber, Airbnb, Spotify, Netflix and similar.
priceDetail: Free (browse all, copy samples only); Pro $12.58/mo billed yearly = $151/yr; Team $450/yr for 3 seats; a Lifetime option exists but no figure published. Self-hosting offered as an alternative.
notes: Fast route from 'what do the best apps do for checkout and onboarding' to editable Figma layers you can restyle into a client's design system - it compresses the reference-gathering and first-draft stage.
The library is a continuous capture operation, not a feature. At ~$151/yr it is far cheaper than staffing the pipeline; the plugin and MCP plumbing is the easy part.

Two cautions. IP: you are copying other companies' UI and trade dress into Figma - fine as internal reference, dangerous if any survives into a client deliverable, so set a house rule that Flaude output gets fully restyled. Vendor risk: solo/indie with no company details, and Pro depends on a hosted MCP; the open-source repo mitigates this only if it actually has a licence, which I could not confirm. Check the plugin's terms before installing on a client-shared Figma org.
adminNote: House rule: Flaude output gets fully restyled before it goes anywhere near a client deliverable.

name: Refero Styles
what: Curated library of 2,000+ machine-readable design systems extracted from real product websites. Each entry exposes colours, type, spacing, components and a DESIGN.md you can drop into Cursor, Claude Code or v0.
priceDetail: Free to browse. Pro subscription required for the MCP/automation path (8,000 tool calls/mo). No price published - get it in writing.
notes: You already store design tokens in Foundry, so machine-readable token sets are a direct input to both design-system work and AI-assisted build.
Scraping computed styles into a DESIGN.md is a couple of days. Curating 2,000 systems is the bit you cannot copy - use theirs, build your own extractor only for client sites.

These are other companies' design systems reverse-engineered from live sites. Fine as reference and benchmarking, dubious as a shortcut for producing a client's brand. Beta, so spot-check spacing/component accuracy. Pricing is opaque - confirm before wiring a workflow to it.
adminNote: Free browsing is a benchmarking reference. Get the Pro price in writing before wiring MCP into a workflow.

name: Transitions.dev
what: Copy-paste library of 36+ production-ready UI transitions (card resize, modal, button, text effects) in CSS and React, plus an agent skill that installs them into a project and a live tuning tool. By Jakub Antalik.
priceDetail: Free tier. Pro $9/mo solo or $149 one-time lifetime. Team $39/mo for 5 seats or $499 lifetime. Commercial licence, unlimited projects.
notes: Motion is the fiddliest, most time-expensive polish layer on client builds. $149 lifetime pays back on one project's animation work.
You could write 36 transitions, but the value is the taste and the tuned easing curves. Recreating that judgement costs far more than $149.

Best value item in the batch. Single maintainer, so lifetime tier carries bus-factor risk - though you own the copied code, so abandonment costs future additions, not working projects. Verify the commercial licence covers redistribution inside client deliverables, not just your own products. Check the free companion repo first.
adminNote: Best value item in the batch. Buy the $149 lifetime, but confirm the commercial licence covers client deliverables first.

name: Wonder (Aquila Labs)
what: AI design tool where you generate and edit UI on a canvas that maps 1:1 to code, exporting production-ready React + Tailwind with no handoff. Exposes an MCP endpoint for coding agents.
priceDetail: Free $0 (3 private files, limited tokens). Pro $16/user/mo billed yearly, includes $20/mo AI tokens. Enterprise custom. Also on X as @usewonder.
notes: Design-and-build plus design systems is your core business, and this targets exactly the Figma-to-code handoff bottleneck.
An equivalent means a canvas engine, layout-to-JSX compiler, AI generation, realtime collaboration and a shader library. Multi-year product company, not an agency side project.

Public Alpha is their own label - expect breaking changes, do not put a client deadline on it. Pro's $20 token allowance is a cap, not unlimited. Figma is not mentioned anywhere, so assume no Figma round-trip, which is a real gap if client work starts in Figma. Unlikely to replace Foundry's token layer.
adminNote: Internal projects only while it is in public alpha — no Figma round-trip, so not for a client deadline.

name: Appllama
what: Design research platform cataloguing the screens of top-grossing iOS apps - around 770 apps and 30,900+ screens, added weekly - so you can study onboarding, paywalls and flows from apps that demonstrably make money, alongside their revenue, download and ratings data. Sold to designers and, explicitly, to AI agents via MCP credits.
priceDetail: Free (welcome screens, 2 newest apps rotating). Pro $12/mo billed yearly ($144/yr) or $20/mo monthly. Team $16/seat/mo annual ($192/yr per seat), 2-seat minimum. Enterprise custom. Pro and Team include 1,500 MCP credits/month.
notes: Strong for the pitch and discovery phase of native app work - 'here is how the top-grossing apps in your category handle paywalls' is a credible proposal input - but it is iOS-only, so it does little for the web builds that are most of your work.
Recreating it means continuously capturing and tagging ~31k screens across 760+ apps and joining them to paid App Store intelligence data - a permanent operations cost that dwarfs $144/yr.

Direct overlap with Flaude: Flaude gives editable Figma layers, Appllama gives screens plus commercial performance data. Paying for both is only justified if you do real native iOS work. The MCP angle is the interesting bit - Foundry or Claude Code could query it during a project - but the 1,500-credit ceiling has no published per-call cost, so budgeting is guesswork until you test it. Same IP caution as Flaude: reference, never a deliverable. Site claims design teams at ChatGPT, Strava and Duolingo as users - unverified social proof. Internal inconsistency between 770 apps (pricing page) and 762+ (homepage), so do not quote a precise number to clients.

name: Doppio (via Toolfolio listing)
what: Browser tool that turns static designs, images or Figma links into animated motion reels from code-based templates. The link itself is just a directory entry for it.
priceDetail: Free (2 projects, 5 credits, 4K export). Starter $29/mo billed quarterly. Power $58/mo quarterly. Power for Life $409 one-time. PAYG $29 per 10 credits.
notes: Solves a real agency chore - turning finished client UI into a polished showreel for case studies and pitches without opening After Effects.
An equivalent needs a browser compositor, template system, headless render farm and 4K encoding. Months of work for pure marketing output, not billable delivery.

No company or founder named on the site. The '5 of 100 remaining' lifetime counter and quarterly-only billing are pre-revenue indie signals - treat continuity risk as real and do not make it a dependency in a client-facing workflow. Credit model gets expensive on a heavy showreel month.

name: Hejour
what: Day-based notes app for Mac and iPhone where every day is a page, days link to each other with @ mentions, and todos carry reminders. Notes stored locally as plain Markdown, synced optionally via your own iCloud - no Hejour servers or accounts. Built solo by Enes Genç.
priceDetail: Free tier with no trial clock (unlimited daily notes, todos, search, iPhone sync, imports; capped at 3 linked days and 2 snippets). Pro $19 pay once, covering Mac and iPhone - unlimited linked days, calendar integration, sync across 3 Macs, images, code blocks, Vim mode, lifetime updates.
notes: Genuinely useful as a personal daily work log - what got done on which client, day by day - but single-user and local-first, so it will never be a shared team system alongside Foundry.
$19 once for a polished, notarised, local-Markdown Mac and iOS app is below the cost of a weekend of your own time, and Foundry already owns the multi-user side of this problem.

Local-first Markdown plus your own iCloud is the real selling point - no lock-in, files stay readable if the app dies. Downside is exactly that: personal tool, no shared workspace, one-person indie project, so treat 'lifetime updates' with the usual scepticism. Distributed via GitHub releases rather than the Mac App Store, which matters if you have device-management policies.

name: LogoCreator (logo-creator.io)
what: Free open-source AI logo generator - enter a company name, pick type, style and colours, get logo variations. Aimed at small businesses and founders.
priceDetail: 2 free credits on sign-in, no paid tier figures published. Self-hostable free with your own Together AI key (billed per image).
notes: Raster AI logo output is not usable as a client brand deliverable. At best a throwaway mood-board or placeholder generator.
It is a thin Next.js wrapper around Flux Pro on Together AI plus Clerk and Upstash. Fork it if you want a branded version, but there is no product here.

Genuinely a wrapper with no moat - value sits entirely in the Flux model and prompt presets. Two agency gotchas: output is bitmap not vector, so no clean SVG for a design system; and generated marks carry trademark and originality risk you should not pass to a paying client. Confirm licence terms before forking commercially.

name: Maccess (with 'Mackie' AI)
what: Despite the name it has nothing to do with accessibility. It is an iPhone app plus a required Mac helper for remote-controlling your Mac - virtual touchpad, keyboard, screen mirroring, file transfer, lock/sleep/restart, and an AI assistant called Mackie that runs automated tasks on the Mac. By Appic Marketing LLC. Needs iOS 17+ and macOS 14+.
priceDetail: Free tier (core touchpad and keyboard control, 1 paired Mac) and a Pro tier (screen mirroring, Mackie AI, unlimited Macs). No price figures published anywhere - you must install the app to see them. Some advanced AI modes need your own Claude Code or provider account.
notes: A personal remote-control convenience tool, not an audit, delivery or client-facing tool. The only agency angle is remotely poking a build machine or a Mac mini running a long task.

A real equivalent means a signed and notarised macOS helper daemon, low-latency screen streaming, Accessibility and Screen Recording entitlements, secure pairing and an iOS client. Expensive and off-mission.

IMPORTANT: the name reads like an accessibility product (Mac + access). It is not. It will not help run WCAG audits on client sites - no contrast checks, no axe or ARIA tooling, nothing. If it landed on an accessibility list it was mis-filed. Second flag: no public pricing at all, and the Mackie assistant executing tasks on your Mac has obvious security implications on a machine holding client code.

name: Path.cv
what: Hosted personal-site builder - upload a PDF CV and it converts to a live site, or build from templates. Includes a browsable public directory of users filterable by skill, location and profession.
priceDetail: Free on a path.cv subdomain. Pro $10/mo, or $6/mo billed annually.
notes: Serves individuals building their own CV site - closer to a downmarket substitute for what you sell than a tool you would use.

A CV-to-templated-site generator is genuinely small for a team with a design system and deploy pipeline, but at $10/mo against Framer, Bento, Super and LinkedIn it is a commodity market with no room for an agency to earn from it.

Two things worth weighing: it is a mild commodity-pressure signal at the very bottom of the market, relevant only if you ever quote cheap one-page personal sites; and the two-sided directory is the only interesting mechanic, but directories are hard to keep alive. Operator undisclosed - treat continuity as uncertain before recommending to a client.

name: TinyFolder
what: Native macOS app that groups applications into custom folders pinned to the Dock so you can open apps from a themed folder with one click. Made solo by Sergey Filkov. Requires macOS 13+.
priceDetail: Starter free - 1 folder, up to 4 apps. Lifetime Pro for 2 Macs $32 once - unlimited folders and apps, full Design Studio, 64 presets, 4 icon packs, global shortcuts, all future updates. 14-day money-back guarantee.
notes: Desktop cosmetics and launcher ergonomics for one machine. Touches nothing in client delivery, design systems or production readiness.
Reimplementing Dock-integrated folders, icon rendering and a preset and theming studio in AppKit is weeks of fiddly native work for a utility costing $32 once.

Worth flagging as a design-craft reference more than a tool: a tightly-scoped indie Mac product with a clean free-to-lifetime upgrade ladder, and a marketing site worth stealing patterns from for productised agency offers. Pro licence covers 2 Macs, so a team needs multiple purchases.

name: Halo (meethalo.app)
what: iPhone-only private AI assistant pulling mail, calendar, reminders, health and music into one daily briefing, triggering actions in third-party apps over MCP, with all processing claimed on-device. Consumer product, not team or agency.
priceDetail: Halo Lifetime $49 early bird, stated regular price $99, one-time, 7-day trial. No subscription tier. Product is not shipping yet.
notes: Single-user consumer iPhone assistant with no client, project or team dimension. Does nothing for agency delivery or Foundry.
Not worth building or copying - an on-device iOS assistant with EventKit/HealthKit/Mail permissions plus an MCP client is a months-long native project, and none of it serves agency ops.

Be sceptical: a pre-launch landing page selling a lifetime licence for a product that is not shipping. $49 upfront for a promise, no App Store listing to check reviews against, no company track record on the page. 'All on-device, no servers' is unverifiable pre-release and sits awkwardly next to the option to configure ChatGPT or Grok as providers. No Android. Several unrelated products are also called Halo.
